segments.caption: The birthday paradox.
Why your gut gets it wrong, the maths step by step, a live simulation, and where it's used in real life. Save this one!
A cricket match. 22 players on the field, plus the umpire. 23 people.
What's the chance that two of them share a birthday?
Most people guess around 6%. 23 out of 365. Comment your guess before the answer.
The real answer? 50.7%. Basically a coin flip.
And with 70 people, it's 99.9%. Almost certain.
Your brain is answering the wrong question. It's thinking: does someone share my birthday?
That really is small: about 6%.
But the question is: do ANY two people share a birthday? And with 23 people, there are 253 different pairs.
Even 5 friends make 10 pairs. Every new person pairs up with everyone already in the room.
That's 253 chances for a match.
It's easier to work out the opposite: everyone has a different birthday.
Person 1 can have any day: 365 out of 365.
Person 2 must avoid that day: 364 out of 365.
Person 3: 363 out of 365. And so on, down to person 23: 343 out of 365.
Each fraction is only a little below 1. But multiply 22 of them, and the total shrinks fast.
Multiply them all, and the chance that everyone is different is only 49.3%.
So the chance of at least one shared birthday is 100 minus 49.3: that's 50.7%.
Watch how fast it climbs.
10 people: 12%. 23 people: 50%. 40 people: 89%. 57 people: 99%.
Still don't believe it? We simulated 1,000 rooms, each with 23 random people.
In 507 of them, two people shared a birthday. Half the rooms, just like the maths said.
And this isn't just a party trick.
Hackers use it. The birthday attack finds two files with the same digital fingerprint much faster than you'd expect. That's why passwords and bank systems use extremely long codes.
And in a class of 60 students? A shared birthday is 99.4% certain.
So remember: when everyone is compared with everyone, the pairs explode, and coincidences become likely.
It's also why lottery results seem to repeat suspiciously often. With enough draws, a repeat is expected.
Save this, and test it in your next group chat.
